title: Rai Kalha
hookLine: a Muslim chief who sheltered the Guru and sent a messenger to learn the children's fate
tomorrow: Mai Bhago, the woman who led

lines: THE GURU, WANTED BY THE EMPIRE.
A CHIEF WITH EVERYTHING TO LOSE.
cards: A door, and a knock, and a choice. On the other side of the door is Guru Gobind Singh, wanted by the empire.

He has come through Chamkaur and Machhiwara, through the forest and the cold, and he doesn't yet know what has happened to his two youngest sons and his mother. On this side of the door is a local chief of Raikot.
He's Muslim. He has lands, a family and a lot to lose. Taking the Guru in means taking a risk with all of it.

teach.b: Rai Kalha opened the door. Tradition says he welcomed Guru Gobind Singh with respect and kept him under his roof, knowing what it could cost.
That's the first thing to hold on to: shelter, given to someone hunted, by a man of another faith. Then he did a second thing, quieter and harder. The Guru wanted news of his family.
Sirhind was dangerous ground, so Rai Kalha sent one of his own men, a messenger tradition names Noora Mahi, to find out.
Riding into the governor's city, asking questions about the Guru's children, then riding back with whatever he learned. And what he learned was the worst news there is.
He told the Guru what had happened at Sirhind: the boys executed, Mata Gujri gone. So Rai Kalha's house is where the Guru heard it. Shelter isn't only a roof.

teach.h: A SAFE PLACE TO HEAR BAD NEWS.
teach.b: Sometimes it's a place safe enough to hear terrible news. Tradition remembers the parting too.
Before he moved on, the Guru gave Rai Kalha a gift in thanks, a vessel his family kept and honored.
Sikhs still speak of Rai Kalha with gratitude, alongside the others who stood near the Guru in those weeks: Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan, the Nawab of Malerkotla, Todar Mal.

In Gurbani, sharan, shelter or refuge, is used for taking refuge in God, and Sikhs speak of coming to the Guru's sharan. In this story, for a few days, the Guru came to someone else's, and was received.

how: Sikhs remember Rai Kalha of Raikot among the people of other faiths who protected Guru Gobind Singh, and his story is told when Sikhs recall the events after Chamkaur and the martyrdom of the younger Sahibzade.

o: the messenger who rode to Sirhind to bring back news
a hill raja who marched against the Guru at Bhangani
the Muslim chief of Raikot who sheltered the hunted Guru

games.q: the house at Raikot — tap the pairs.
p: the boys and Mata Gujri were gone

s: Rai Kalha was a Sikh soldier of the Guru
he was a Muslim chief of Raikot who took the Guru in.
the Guru learned of his sons' deaths while sheltering with Rai Kalha
tradition says Rai Kalha's messenger brought the news from Sirhind.
sharan, shelter, is also a Gurbani word for refuge in God
people come to the Guru's sharan; here the Guru came to someone else's.

games.q: you're Rai Kalha. the Guru under your roof needs news from Sirhind, where asking questions is dangerous. what do you do?
o: tell him it's too risky to ask.
send one of your own men to find out.
wait until news reaches Raikot on its own.
games.why: tradition says he sent a messenger, Noora Mahi, who came back with the news of the children.

practice: Picture your own door, the real one, and ask who might be knocking on it this week: a friend whose news is bad, a relative who doesn't feel welcome anywhere.
Think of one form of shelter you could offer, a seat at your table, a phone you'll pick up, a place to hear hard news without being alone. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Rai Kalha. The Muslim chief of Raikot who sheltered Guru Gobind Singh and sent a messenger to Sirhind to learn the children's fate. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: shelter, refuge. Gurbani uses the form ਸਰਣਿ for taking refuge in God.

carryVoice: Your line: he gave shelter. A roof, and a safe place to hear the worst. Until tomorrow.
